name: Wei Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm crew lead for a company that builds mass-timber buildings, mostly with CLT, which is cross-laminated timber: big glued panels of wood that come off a truck and go up like a kit. We're doing a seven-storey student housing block right now, and my crew of five sets the wall and floor panels, screws them off and seals the joints. My day starts at half six with the crane lift plan on my phone, then it's hand signals, impact drivers and checking levels with the laser. I love how quiet a timber site is compared to concrete; the bit that wears me out is when a panel arrives cut wrong and the whole sequence falls over.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned your phone for the lift plan. How much do you use tech day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Loads. I use an AI assistant every day, for checking the panel schedule against the drawings, writing up snag lists from my voice notes, and translating for Tiago and Marek on my crew when it gets technical. I also built a little spreadsheet that flags which screws we're running low on. My partner Sam works in city planning and teases me that I'm a nerd in a hard hat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold, which is roughly what I think now. I'd probably post a thread about the ways it actually helped me on site, the snag lists and translation, and the ways it didn't. Most of the hype people don't know what a crane day looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I've got a slight edge over the guys who never touched it, and that's about it. I'd keep building good timber buildings, and the housing crisis means there's no shortage of work. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant and probably push my boss to pay for a better version for all the crew leads. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month aside. And I'd go on with my plan to do the mass-timber installer certification next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit disappointed, if I'm honest, because I like the shiny stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed? Say more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd half been hoping AI would sort out the boring parts of building, like the endless paperwork and the clashes in the drawings. That's where most of my bad days come from. If it stays a slightly better search engine, I'm still fighting the same paperwork in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the rest of your crew think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek would be delighted, he thinks it's all nonsense anyway. Tiago would miss the translation, I think, it's made him a lot more confident speaking up on site.

S0.say: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold, and I'd post a thread about how it really helped on site and where it didn't. Most hype people have never seen a crane day.
S0.think: Privately it means I keep a slight edge over people who never touched it, and that's all. The housing crisis means plenty of timber work anyway.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI assistant daily and asks his boss to pay for a better version for all crew leads. Keeps saving a few hundred a month and takes the mass-timber installer certification next spring.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small disappointment that the boring paperwork won't get fixed.
S0.quote: If it stays a slightly better search engine, I'm still fighting the same paperwork in ten years.
S0.fieldNote: An enthusiastic daily user who is mildly let down by the plateau. He sees AI's value in admin and in helping his migrant crew members speak up. No sense of threat at all in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be great for builders if workers get a share of the gains, through shorter hours or better pay instead of fewer jobs. I'd say it on site and online. I'd be pushing the union to stop just saying no and start bargaining over how the tools get used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out ahead. Mass timber is already half factory, half site, and the people who understand both and can work with the software are going to be needed. I'd be the guy who runs the robot crane rather than the guy it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on the pilot when the company trials any automated tools, like the panel-placing robots they've shown at trade fairs. I'd do an online course in reading BIM models, that's the 3D building models the designers use, so I can talk to the office on their terms. I might also put a bit of savings into a friend's small business that does timber retrofits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. I'd want to be in the room when it changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, honestly. He's brilliant with his hands but he won't touch a tablet, and if the job becomes half screen, he's going to get squeezed. I'd want to bring him along with me, not leave him behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you bring him along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pair him with the tech on site and let me handle the screen side while he does the fine work. Every crew still needs someone who can feel when a joint's wrong. I'd argue for that to the boss.

S1.say: I'd say this could be great for builders if workers share the gains through shorter hours or better pay, not fewer jobs. I'd push the union to bargain over how the tools get used instead of just saying no.
S1.think: Off the record I think I'd come out ahead: mass timber is half factory, half site, and people who understand both plus the software will be needed. I'd run the robot crane, not be replaced by it.
S1.do: Volunteers for any company pilot of automated tools such as panel-placing robots and takes an online course in reading BIM building models. Considers putting some savings into a friend's timber retrofit business.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, wanting to be in the room when it changes, with concern for his less tech-minded colleague.
S1.quote: I'd be the guy who runs the robot crane rather than the guy it replaces.
S1.fieldNote: He positions himself as a bridge between the screen and the hands. His progressive outlook shows as a push for shared gains rather than resistance. Genuinely protective of Marek, whom he expects to get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to fight for public ownership of the gains, a dividend for everyone, because if a handful of companies own all the robots we're done. I'd be loud about it online and I'd be organising. I'd also say, to anyone who'd listen, that the tools themselves aren't evil, the ownership is the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even I'd be shaken. Two years is barely enough to get good at the new tools before they don't need anyone running them. My adaptability buys me maybe a year or two of extra work, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd jump on whatever the robot install crews need, the operators and checkers, and squeeze as much pay out of those last couple of years as I could. I'd put more aside, maybe double my savings, and stop paying for the climbing gym. And I'd join the campaign for a public AI dividend, probably helping run its social media, because that's what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the technology and scared of who owns it, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say "you're the one who plans cities, so you'd better plan one where nobody needs a job". She'd laugh and then she'd go quiet. She's already worried about her own office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're good at adapting. Is that a comfort here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than I'd like. Being adaptable is great when there's a new thing to adapt to. When the new thing does everything, it's like being the fastest runner in a race that's been cancelled.

S2.say: I'd say this is the moment to fight for public ownership of the gains, a dividend for everyone, because if a handful of firms own the robots we're done. The tools aren't evil; the ownership is the problem.
S2.think: Privately even I'd be shaken. Two years barely lets me master the new tools before they need nobody running them, so adaptability buys a year or two of work, not a career.
S2.do: Moves onto robot install crews as an operator or checker and earns all he can in the last couple of years. Doubles his savings, drops the climbing gym and helps run social media for a public AI dividend campaign.
S2.feel: Anxious, excited by the technology and scared of who owns it at the same time.
S2.quote: It's like being the fastest runner in a race that's been cancelled.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-comfortable worker here sees his adaptability as a short-term edge, not protection. His anger targets ownership rather than technology. He'd put his digital skills into campaigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up a fair system, so let's not waste three of them arguing. Shorter working weeks, a citizen's dividend, worker seats on company boards. I'd say that loudly, at union meetings and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me better than most. I'd have time to move from installer to someone who sets up and maintains robot crews, and maybe after that into designing the sequences they follow. I'd be riding the wave for a while, even knowing it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do a course in robotics for construction, there's a part-time one at the technical college. I'd ask to lead the first robot pilot on our sites, and I'd keep saving a bit more. By 2029 or so, I'd want a few mates and me to set up a small co-op that runs robot crews ourselves, so the profit stays with workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly, with some real excitement mixed in. It's the feeling before a big crane lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A co-op of robot crews. Where would the money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings from the five of us, maybe twenty thousand between us, and a loan from a co-op bank. I don't actually know if it would work. But it's better than watching a big firm buy the machines and pocket everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to learn the machines properly and time to own a bit of them. Two years, I'm a passenger. Five, I might get a hand on the wheel.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years to set up a fair system: shorter working weeks, a citizen's dividend and worker seats on company boards. I'd say it at union meetings and online.
S3.think: Off the record, five years suits me better than most: I'd move from installer to setting up and maintaining robot crews, maybe designing their sequences. I'd ride the wave knowing it ends.
S3.do: Takes a part-time robotics for construction course at the technical college in the first year and asks to lead the first robot pilot. Saves more and plans, around 2029, a worker co-op with friends running its own robot crews, funded by about 20,000 in pooled savings and a co-op bank loan.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with real excitement mixed in.
S3.quote: Two years, I'm a passenger. Five, I might get a hand on the wheel.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns him into a would-be owner of the machines. His co-op idea combines progressive politics with adaptive risk-taking. He's honest that he doesn't know if it would work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, so let's use it to build a society where AGI means less work for everyone, not no income for most. I'd be campaigning for a four-day week now, as a first step. I'd tell people to learn the tools, but to vote too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right through most of it and then face the same wall at thirty-seven as everybody else. But by then I'd hope the politics had moved. That's the real bet I'm making, more than any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course, then spend a few years really good at robot crews, and set up the co-op around 2032 instead of rushing it. I'd keep saving and maybe buy a small flat with Sam, as long as the mortgage is short. I'd get properly involved in a political party, local branch stuff, because ten years is enough time to change who's in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. I can see a version of this that's actually good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the good version look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I build things I care about three days a week, with robots doing the lifting, and spend the rest of the time climbing and teaching kids carpentry. Everyone gets a share from the machines. It sounds daft said out loud, but I think it's possible if we fight for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the bad version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five companies own everything and I'm doing delivery shifts for a robot firm. That's the one that keeps me up. The decade is what decides which one we get.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is a gift: let's build a society where AGI means less work for everyone, not no income for most. I'd campaign for a four-day week now and tell people to learn the tools but also vote.
S4.think: Privately I'd be fine through most of it, then hit the same wall at thirty-seven as everyone. My real bet is that the politics will have moved by then, more than any course.
S4.do: Takes the robotics course, works on robot crews for a few years and sets up the worker co-op around 2032. Keeps saving, perhaps buys a flat with Sam on a short mortgage, and gets involved in his local party branch.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, able to picture a version of the future that is genuinely good.
S4.quote: Five companies own everything and I'm doing delivery shifts for a robot firm. That's the one that keeps me up.
S4.fieldNote: He sees the decade as a political contest more than a personal one. His hopeful picture is concrete: three days building, the rest climbing and teaching. Both his optimism and his fear rest on who ends up owning the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to change who owns anything. What would help is a public dividend from AI that pays everyone, set up before it lands. And worker co-ops getting cheap loans to buy the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd enjoy about it. I genuinely think robots carrying the heavy panels could save a lot of backs and knees. I just want the people whose backs it saves to still be eating.

headlineQuote: I just want the people whose backs it saves to still be eating.
portrait: Wei is a 27-year-old crew lead on mass-timber buildings who uses an AI assistant every day for snag lists, schedules and translating for his crew. He is curious, comfortable with risk and excited by the technology, but his progressive politics make ownership of the machines his central question. He is calm in the mild pictures and sees himself coming out ahead. Fast AGI leaves him anxious, aware that adaptability only buys a year or two; with five or ten years he plans to run robot crews and set up a worker co-op that owns them. His hope and his fear both depend on whether the gains are shared.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to change who owns the machines and the gains.
whatWouldHelp: A public AI dividend paying everyone, set up before it lands, and cheap loans for worker co-ops to buy the machines.
